question: to the Commission Roman Haider (PfE), Tom Vandendriessche (PfE), Elisabeth Dieringer (PfE), Ondřej Knotek (PfE), Jaroslava Pokorná Jermanová (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Mary Khan (ESN), Tomasz Froelich (ESN), Siegbert Frank Droese (ESN), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN), Alexander Sell (ESN), Ivan David (ESN), Irmhild Boßdorf (ESN), Zsuzsanna Borvendég (ESN), Markus Buchheit (ESN), Kosma Złotowski (ECR), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Adrian-George Axinia (ECR), Paolo Inselvini (ECR), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI), Branko Grims (PPE), Christine Anderson (ESN), Alexander Jungbluth (ESN) Subject:

Year after year, the Commission pours millions into projects, campaigns and public awareness activities. Whole strategies are dedicated to increasing visibility for gender identities – underpinned by support programmes, training and EU-wide guidelines. This policy has now become ubiquitous, from educational establishments to government departments. Brussels is financing pride campaigns, while the role of families as essential pillars of society is ignored. This massive imbalance is not only unjust; it is a political warning signal. A society that neglects families politically and financially puts its own future in jeopardy. While millions are being mobilised across the EU for specific interest groups, parents, who are responsible for children, often come away empty-handed. Anyone who tries to fob mothers and fathers off with purely symbolic policies, while wholeheartedly endorsing pride initiatives, is prioritising ideology over their social responsibility. 1.
Going forward, does the Commission intend to promote the societal image of family and parenthood just as actively as that of minority groups?
Does the Commission have a dedicated strategy for promoting and showcasing family, parenthood and children as essential pillars of society, comparable to the LGBTQ equality strategy?

What criteria is the Commission using to assess the impact of LGBTQ public awareness campaigns with regard to effectiveness, reach and societal acceptance, and are these same criteria used when assessing campaigns or initiatives that promote families?

(30 June 2026) EU policies and funding instruments aim to support and empower families across the EU with key objectives, including the promotion of equality, supporting work-life balance and conciliation, enhancing child well-being and combating poverty and social exclusion. This is reflected in initiatives like the European Pillar of Social Right s (1), the Gender Equality Strategy (2), the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy (3), the strategy for the rights of persons with disabilities (4), the European Care Strategy (5) and the EU strategy on the rights of the child (6). The responsibility for shaping family policy and broader societal choices regarding family life and parenthood rests primarily with the Member States. Within the limits of its competences and in full respect of the principle of subsidiarity, the Commission supports families through different measures. For example, via the EU Cohesion Policy funds, or the European Child Guarantee (7), the Commission provides support for home care and family care systems, for services for children, young people and families to promote their well-being, and for the participation of children in early childhood education and care for families at risk of poverty.

The Commission applies standard evaluation frameworks across its programmes (typically relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, reach and impact), including for awareness-raising initiatives. For all its awareness-raising campaigns, the Commission measures outputs (e.g. reach), results (e.g. campaign recall) and impacts (e.g. percentage of audience reached having a more positive opinion of the campaign’s topic) following the Commission Communication Indicators, of which the details can be consulted online (8).
